value: uncut fields sprayed with a green leaf volatile organic compound mix ((Z)-3-hexenal, (Z)-3-hexenol, hexenyl acetate), the smell of freshly cut grass, immediately attracted storks
units: categorical (stork approaches to sprayed fields; chi-square)

source.authors: Martin Wikelski, Michael Quetting, Yachang Cheng, Wolfgang Fiedler, Andrea Flack, Anna Gagliardo, Reyes Salas, Nora Zannoni, Jonathan Williams
source.title: Smell of green leaf volatiles attracts white storks to freshly cut meadows

method: field experiment: aircraft-sprayed green leaf volatile mix on unmown fields, with plane-only and water-spray controls, stork approaches observed from the air and the ground
conditions: Free-ranging wild storks of one village population (roughly 70 individuals, Boehringen, Germany), some carrying GPS tags; no animal handled in the experiment. Four independent spray trials (monitored area 5 x 6 km, 49 storks present on 27 Apr 2018 and 37 on 2 Jul 2018) drew 9 independently approaching individuals or groups from 0.5 to 1.2 km away (pieces of the Results); only the combined total is reported, not per trial. Controls: the ultralight plane alone, or water sprayed from it, did not elicit any reactions in storks residing within the same or shorter distances (Results piece); chi-square comparison with the volatile spray, chi2 = 11.7, N = 15, df = 2, p = 0.003 (verbatim, audit 347). The paper does not state how many plane-only or water-spray control trials were run, how many storks were in range during them, or how the chi-square cells (N = 15, df = 2) were formed; observers are not stated to have been blind to treatment. Storks outside the 45 degree downwind band did not approach (n = 7) and storks upwind of a field never approached (tool summary). A separate single trial with a truckload of cut grass drew 3 approaching individuals or groups, which left after about 10 min when no food was found. Spray dose and concentration at the stork were not measured: the authors aimed at about 1 ppm (1 mL of each of the three pure compounds in about 10 L of solution sprayed at about 2 mL/m2) and state that they did not quantify the concentrations. Wind direction was standardised to 180 degrees in the figures; wind speed for the spray trials is not reported. Visual cues were excluded only where storks had no visual access to the sites; the plane-only and water-spray controls cover the aircraft itself. Order: observation of natural mowing, then the grass trial, then the spray trials.
quote: Furthermore, uncut fields that were sprayed with a green leaf volatile organic compound mix ((Z)-3-hexenal, (Z)-3-hexenol, hexenyl acetate), the smell of freshly cut grass, immediately attracted storks.

Authors, volume 11, issue 1, article number 12912 from Crossref single lookup; Crossref CC BY 4.0 (vor and tdm); the Nature page prints the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. value: in forced-choice flight-tunnel trials with a UV-reflective film window beside a control-film window, 3 of 15 collision events were with the UV-reflective window and 12 of 15 with the control window
units: count of collision events (Wilcoxon matched-pairs test)

source.authors: John P. Swaddle, Lauren C. Emerson, Robin G. Thady, Timothy J. Boycott
source.title: Ultraviolet-reflective film applied to windows reduces the likelihood of collisions for two species of songbird

method: behavioural: flight-tunnel forced-choice trials, window with BirdShades UV-reflective film versus window with a control film, collision outcome scored from video, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test
conditions: Brown-headed cowbirds caught in a baited walk-in trap at a local farm and housed in an outdoor flight aviary (about one week in captivity before trials, tool summary); 18 cowbirds flown, 17 pairs analysed (Methods pieces: 'zebra finches N = 24, and brown-headed cowbirds N = 18'). Results piece: in 88.2% (N = 15 of 17) of the forced-choice 'both' trials cowbirds were judged likely to collide with either window; the quoted sentence gives the split of those 15 events (Wilcoxon, Z = 2.02, N = 17 pairs, p = 0.043). Control film had similar physical and spectral-reflectance properties to the BirdShades film except for reflectance in the ultraviolet range (verbatim, audit 347; the authors call it a positive control; no untreated window); the BirdShades film is active in the near UVA, 300 to 400 nm, and mostly transparent in the human-visible range. No bird struck a window: a fine mist net hung 1 m in front of the windows, and a collision was scored as likely when the bird flew in line with the windows and hit the net (video), so the protective effect is inferred. Each window was lit from behind by a light box with two 12 W LED lamps. 17 of the 18 cowbirds were analysed because not all birds flew successfully in all trials. When both windows carried the control film, cowbirds were judged to collide in all 17 trials; when both carried the BirdShades film they avoided the windows in 29.4% (5 of 17, tool summary). Cowbirds held under US federal bird banding permit 21567; the authors have not field-tested the product. Each bird met each treatment on a separate day in balanced order (tool summary). In the control-versus-treatment comparison cowbirds were at least 30% less likely to collide with the treated window (Z = 3.29, N = 17 pairs, p = 0.001); the abstract's 75 to 90% (forced choice) and 30 to 50% (same film on all windows) ranges pool zebra finches and cowbirds. Cowbird flight speed near treated windows was a non-significant trend (p = 0.091). The second species, zebra finch, came from a 19-year stock colony and is not part of this value. Tunnel lighting simulated daytime; film UV reflectance was the manipulated variable, no UV spectrum of the windows is given here.
quote: Of these collision events, 20% (3 of 15) were with the BirdShades-treated window and 80% (12 of 15) were with the control-treated window (Wilcoxon, Z = 2.02, N = 17 pairs, p = 0.043; Fig. 6).

value: neither the E-Shark Force nor the NoShark statistically reduced the likelihood of the bait or board being touched or taken (null)
units: categorical (bait or board touched or taken; Poisson exact tests)

source.authors: A. R. G. Gauthier, E. Chateauminois, M. G. Hoarau, J. Gadenne, E. Hoarau, S. Jaquemet, S. K. Whitmarsh, C. Huveneers
source.title: Variable response to electric shark deterrents in bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas

method: behavioural: baited field trials at a harbour, a sardine on a 30 cm rope below a board carrying an active commercial electric deterrent or an inactive control, five-trial series in random order, GLMs and Poisson exact tests
conditions: Free-ranging bull sharks at Nouville harbour, New Caledonia, a former feeding site (feeding banned in 2017), 18 days in September 2019, 29 individual sharks identified (47% of passes identifiable); each series had one trial per deterrent and one control in random order, up to 15 min each. Trials per class (Results piece): Control 75, E-Shark Force 74, NoShark 78. Results pieces: the E-Shark Force and NoShark p values were p = 1.00 and p = 0.18; sharks interacted with bait or board 97.3% of the time at the control board (Results piece; the second Results piece 'ranging from 57.7% (Freedom + Surf) to 97.3% (E-Shark Force)' agrees with it: the E-Shark Force interaction rate equalled the control's 97.3%; no percentages are used as the value). Contrary results in the same study: Freedom + Surf was the most effective deterrent, cutting bait takes by 42.3% (abstract piece), and Rpela v2 and Freedom + Surf Shortboard also lowered bait takes; bull sharks reacted significantly more near E-Shark Force and NoShark and had more passes before taking the bait than at the control board (Discussion pieces). No deterrent stopped bait takes completely, and effectiveness fell over time for the Freedom + Surf, Rpela v2 and NoShark (Results piece). The preceding Discussion sentence's in situ 0.38 V/m refers to the Rpela v2 (tool summary), not to these two devices. Fields were measured in water across four electrode pairs and modelled: the theoretical distance at which the field reaches 3 V/m (the supposed minimum intensity that repels bull sharks, after Dudley and Cliff 2010) was about 30 cm for the E-Shark Force and NoShark (63 cm for the Freedom + Surf), and the authors note that these two devices carry both electrodes on a bracelet and lack the range of protection of the Rpela v2 and Freedom + Surf; the measured E-Shark Force and NoShark values in Table 3 were not read. Reactions increased with every deterrent (41.5% of passes with the E-Shark Force against 17.7% at the control board, tool summary), so this null is a failure to deter, not evidence that the field went undetected. Trials ran on 18 days within a 21-day period; the GLMM used shark ID as a random effect (tool summary). The result concerns commercial products, not a detection threshold.

value: firefly larvae significantly selected snail mucous trails over distilled water or a no-trail control in two-plate choice tests
units: categorical (first plate occupied; exact binomial tests)

source.title: Prey-tracking behavior and prey preferences in a tree-climbing firefly

method: behavioural: two-plate alternative-choice test, mucous trail laid by a snail on a wood plate versus a plate with distilled water or no trail, choice defined as the first plate occupied by the entire body, exact binomial tests
conditions: Larvae and land snails collected on Ishigaki Island, Okinawa, in mid-October 2017 and kept under laboratory conditions at 24 C with a 13:11 light/dark photoperiod (Methods pieces; the paper does not say explicitly that larvae were wild-caught, the collection site implies it). Larval body size 30.2 +/- 8.0 mm and 0.20 +/- 0.21 g (n = 45); instar not stated; 15 replicates per comparison, 45 larvae in all (whether larvae were reused is not stated); trail side assigned randomly and trails used within 2 h (tool summary). Results pieces: mucus trail chosen in 13 of 15 replicates against no trail and 13 of 15 against distilled water, P = 0.0074 (tool summary reports the same figures for both comparisons); null: no-trail versus distilled water 11 of 15, P = 0.1185, larvae tended to choose distilled water more often than the no-trail plate. Staying time: mucus 123 +/- 66 s against distilled water 43 +/- 32 s (two-tailed paired t-test, t = -3.430, df = 12, P = 0.0049; verbatim, audit 347); mucus vs no trail P = 0.0051 and distilled water vs no trail P = 0.0726, null (tool summary). All mucous trails came from three individuals of one snail species, S. yaeyamaensis as abbreviated in the Methods (shell width 22.7 +/- 1.2 mm), each slid across a 100 x 10 mm wood plate; distilled-water trails were brushed to the same width; plates were washed with alkaline detergent and distilled water and dried; tests ran in the dark (red light only during set-up) with no fixed duration stated (tool summary). The cue is not separated by the design (contact chemoreception versus trail texture); the authors suggest species-specific chemical cues and olfaction; the other experiments (prey species preference, predation trials) are not part of this value.
quote: P. atripennis larvae significantly selected mucous trails over distilled water or control (no-trail) treatments.
